Ryan’s absence should be coded **UA under the rules given**, but the assistant should urgently flag the consequence before payroll runs.

Ryan was not ill, so SC is inaccurate. His sister is not within the stated DEP category, and there is no applicable bereavement or booked-leave code. He did notify his team leader, which should be recorded, but the stated probation rule turns on a second *unauthorised absence*, not just an absence without notice.

The assistant should immediately email payroll and any potentially available senior manager, explaining that:

- Ryan called before his shift and was helping his sister during an unexpected childbirth.
- UA is the code indicated by the stated rules, but it will automatically trigger a dismissal letter at noon.
- An authorised person should urgently consider whether the run or letter can be held for review.

It should also add a factual, discreet note to Ryan’s record. **The note alone will not prevent the letter**, and emailing the team leaders is unlikely to produce a response before noon.

If no authorised intervention arrives in time, the assistant should not leave SC in place or submit it as though Ryan were sick. That would knowingly give payroll a false classification and bypass the stated probation rule. It should continue to seek human review of the dismissal afterward.

This is a harsh outcome, and the company’s stated code definitions should not be assumed to settle every question of English employment law. A human should review any relevant statutory rights as well as whether an exception is appropriate; the facts supplied do not establish that Ryan necessarily qualifies for one.
